mainTopic: The story of הורדוס rebuilding the בית המקדש, then the משנה's rules on shared walls, partitions in gardens and fields, and the חזית mark
overview: This amud finishes the story of הורדוס and בבא בן בוטא. הורדוס comes in disguise and tries to get the blind חכם to curse the king, but he refuses every time, backing each refusal with a פסוק. הורדוס reveals himself and asks how to make up for killing the חכמים. בבא בן בוטא tells him to rebuild the בית המקדש and gives him a plan to get past רומי. The גמרא praises the beautiful marble building and asks how בבא בן בוטא could advise a wicked king, when דניאל was punished for advising נבוכדנצר. It answers in two ways and proves that דניאל was punished. Then the גמרא returns to the משנה about a shared wall: local custom decides the material, a fallen wall belongs to both neighbors, and רבא explains when a garden or a field needs a partition. Finally the גמרא discusses the חזית, the mark on a wall built by one neighbor, and begins רבי יוחנן's explanation, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: הורדוס blinds בבא בן בוטא
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס puts a crown of porcupine hide on בבא בן בוטא's head, and it pokes out his eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: He put a crown of porcupine hide around his head, and it pierced his eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: הורדוס spared בבא בן בוטא's life but blinded him in a cruel way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, הורדוס killed the חכמים and left only בבא בן בוטא alive. Here we learn the price of being spared: he was made blind. This sets up the test that follows, where הורדוס comes to him in disguise.

keyTerms.meaning: a crown or wreath worn around the head
porcupines (here, a crown made of their spiky hide)

phrases.english: He put around him a crown of porcupine hide,
phrases.notes: The one doing this is הורדוס, and 'him' is בבא בן בוטא.

phrases.english: and it pierced his eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of הורדוס from before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הורדוס blinded בבא בן בוטא, the only חכם he left alive.

steps.title: הורדוס, in disguise, urges him to curse the king
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס sits before the blind בבא בן בוטא without saying who he is, complains about 'this evil slave', and tells him to curse him.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day he came and sat before him. He said: 'See, master, what this evil slave is doing!' He answered: 'What should I do to him?' He said: 'Let the master curse him!'
steps.whatsHappening: הורדוס sets a trap to see whether the blind חכם will speak badly about the king. This line sets up the back-and-forth that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because בבא בן בוטא is blind, he does not know who is talking to him. הורדוס calls himself 'the evil slave' because he really was a former slave. He wants to see whether a חכם would curse the king behind his back.

keyTerms.meaning: see, master (a polite way to address a חכם)

phrases.english: One day he came and sat before him,
he said: See, master,

phrases.aramaic: הַאי עַבְדָּא בִּישָׁא מַאי קָא עָבֵיד!
phrases.english: what this evil slave is doing!
phrases.notes: He is talking about himself, הורדוס, but בבא בן בוטא can't see who is speaking.

phrases.english: He said to him: What should I do to him?
He said to him: Let the master curse him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the blinding, הורדוס comes to test the man he blinded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הורדוס tries to get בבא בן בוטא to curse the king.

steps.title: Refusal: do not curse a king even in thought
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא refuses, quoting the פסוק that forbids cursing a king even in your thoughts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is written, 'Do not curse the king, not even in your thoughts.'
steps.whatsHappening: בבא בן בוטא turns down the suggestion and backs his refusal with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even thinking a curse against a king is wrong, then saying one out loud is certainly wrong. This is the first of several refusals, and each one is based on a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: it is written (a פסוק is being quoted)

phrases.english: He said to him: It is written:
"Even in your thoughts, do not curse a king."
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:20

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the request to curse.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole idea of cursing the king.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The Torah forbids cursing a king, even in one's thoughts.

steps.title: הורדוס objects: he is not a real king
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס argues that the פסוק does not apply, because this ruler is not a real king.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This one is not a king!
steps.whatsHappening: הורדוס pushes back by saying the rule about kings does not cover him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection goes after the foundation of the refusal. If הורדוס is not a lawful king, then the פסוק about a מלך should not stop anyone from cursing him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַאי לָאו מֶלֶךְ הוּא!
phrases.english: He said to him: This one is not a king!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the פסוק cited in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of the פסוק about a king.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: הורדוס is not a lawful king, so the ban on cursing a king does not cover him.

steps.title: Even a rich man or a leader may not be cursed
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא answers that even if he were only a rich man, or only a leader, there is a פסוק against cursing him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Let him be just a rich man, and it is written, 'In your bedroom do not curse a rich man.' And let him be no more than a leader, and it is written, 'Do not curse a leader among your people.'
steps.whatsHappening: בבא בן בוטא gives two fallback reasons, so his refusal holds up even if הורדוס is not a king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not argue about whether הורדוס is a king. He shows that two lower titles, עשיר (rich man) and נשיא (leader), also come with a ban on cursing. Either way, the curse is forbidden.

phrases.english: He said to him: Let him be merely a rich man,
and it is written: "And in your bedroom do not curse a rich man";
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:20

phrases.english: and let him be no more than a leader,
and it is written: "And a leader among your people you shall not curse."
phrases.notes: שמות 22:27

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Fallback sources: even lower categories are protected.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he is not a king, cursing him is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: As a rich man or as a leader, he still may not be cursed.

steps.title: הורדוס objects: he does not act like your people
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס argues that the leader protected by the פסוק is one who acts like a proper member of the Jewish people, and this ruler does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That is about one who acts the way your people act, and this one does not act the way your people act!
steps.whatsHappening: הורדוס attacks the נשיא source by narrowing what 'among your people' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'among your people' (בעמך) are read as a condition: only a leader who behaves according to the תורה is protected. A wicked ruler like הורדוס would not qualify. This leaves the refusal without its last textual support.

keyTerms.meaning: one who acts the way your people act (keeps the Torah)

phrases.english: He said to him: That is about one who acts as your people act,
phrases.notes: He is reading the word 'among your people' in the last פסוק as a condition.

phrases.english: and this one does not act as your people act!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the נשיא source in step 5.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק protects only a leader who behaves like a proper Jew, and הורדוס does not.

steps.title: I am afraid of him
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא switches to a practical reason: he is afraid of the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am afraid of him.
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of arguing about the פסוק, בבא בן בוטא gives a new reason not to curse: fear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not answer the textual argument. He moves to a practical concern, which is that cursing a dangerous ruler could bring punishment.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am afraid of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 by moving to a practical reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A shift from a textual reason to a practical one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With no פסוק stopping him, he should curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fear of the king is still a reason not to.

steps.title: הורדוס objects: no one will tell him
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס says there is nothing to fear, since only the two of them are present.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There is no one who will go and tell him, since only you and I are sitting here.
steps.whatsHappening: הורדוס tries to remove the fear by pointing out that no one else is listening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fear only makes sense if word could get back to the king. With nobody else in the room, הורדוס says, the danger is gone.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֵיכָּא אִינִישׁ דְּאָזֵיל דְּלֵימָא לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: There is no one who will go and tell him,
since only you and I are sitting here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fear given in step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No one else is present, so no one can report the curse.

steps.title: A bird of the sky will carry the sound
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא quotes a פסוק teaching that words spoken in private still get out.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is written, 'For a bird of the sky will carry the sound, and a winged creature will tell the matter.'
steps.whatsHappening: He answers that words spoken in secret find their way out, as the פסוק says.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This finishes the same פסוק in קהלת that he quoted at the start. In total he has quoted three parts of one verse, and he never lets himself curse the king.
steps.whatToRemember: בבא בן בוטא refuses to curse הורדוס at every stage: king, rich man, leader, fear, privacy. Each refusal is backed by a פסוק or by caution.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is written:
"For a bird of the sky will carry the sound,
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:20, the same פסוק as before.

phrases.english: and a winged creature will tell the matter."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם יוֹלִיךְ אֶת הַקּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 and ends the test.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A פסוק showing that private speech gets out.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even private words reach the king, so he still will not curse.

steps.title: הורדוס reveals himself and asks how to repent
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס admits who he is, regrets killing the חכמים, and asks what he can do to fix it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am he. Had I known the Rabbis were this careful, I would not have killed them. Now, what is that man's remedy?
steps.whatsHappening: The test is over. הורדוס reveals himself and asks for a way to do תשובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seeing how carefully the חכם guarded his words, הורדוס understands that the חכמים were never a threat to him. He speaks of himself as 'that man' and asks what his remedy is.

keyTerms.meaning: his remedy, his way to fix it

phrases.english: He said to him: I am he.
phrases.notes: Meaning, I am the king you refused to curse.

phrases.aramaic: אִי הֲוַאי יָדַעְנָא דִּזְהִרִי רַבָּנַן כּוּלֵּי הַאי,
phrases.english: Had I known that the Rabbis are so careful,
I would not have killed them;
now, what is the remedy for that man?
phrases.notes: 'That man' is a polite way of saying 'me'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the test, the story turns to repentance.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can הורדוס make up for killing the חכמים?

steps.title: You put out the light of the world, so work on the light of the world
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא says that since הורדוס put out Torah's light by killing the חכמים, he should work on the בית המקדש, which is also called light.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He put out the light of the world, as it says, 'A מצוה is a lamp and תורה is light.' Let him go and work on the light of the world, as it says, 'And all the nations will stream to it.'
steps.whatsHappening: בבא בן בוטא gives the remedy: rebuild the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The remedy fits the sin. Killing the חכמים put out the 'light' of תורה, so he should take care of another 'light', the בית המקדש. The word ונהרו (stream) in the second פסוק hints at נהורא, light.

keyTerms.meaning: and they will stream (hinting at light)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הוּא כִּבָּה אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם,
phrases.english: He said to him: He put out the light of the world,
as it is written: "For a מצוה is a lamp and Torah is light",
phrases.notes: משלי 6:23

phrases.english: let him go and occupy himself with the light of the world,
phrases.notes: This 'light' is the בית המקדש.

phrases.english: as it is written: "And all the nations will stream to it."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 2:2

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Rebuild the בית המקדש, the 'light of the world', to make up for putting out the light of Torah.

steps.title: Another version: you blinded the eye of the world
steps.stepSummary: Another version: הורדוס blinded the 'eye of the world', the חכמים, so he should work on the 'eye of the world', the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say this is what he told him: He blinded the eye of the world, as it says, 'If by the eyes of the congregation.' Let him go and work on the eye of the world, as it says, 'I will desecrate My Sanctuary, the pride of your strength, the delight of your eyes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the same answer, built on the image of 'eyes' instead of 'light'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice is the same: rebuild the בית המקדש. Only the parallel changes. The חכמים are called the eyes of the community, and the בית המקדש is called the delight of your eyes.

phrases.english: Some say this is what he said to him:
He blinded the eye of the world,
as it is written: "And it shall be, if by the eyes of the congregation",
phrases.notes: במדבר 15:24

phrases.english: let him go and occupy himself with the eye of the world,
as it is written: "Behold, I will desecrate My Sanctuary,
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 24:21

phrases.english: the pride of your strength, the delight of your eyes."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of the answer in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Same remedy, rebuilding the בית המקדש, based on the image of 'eyes'.

steps.title: הורדוס objects: I am afraid of the government of רומי
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס worries that רומי will not let him take down and rebuild the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am afraid of the government.
steps.whatsHappening: הורדוס raises a practical obstacle to the advice he was just given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הורדוס ruled under רומי, so a major project like this needed permission. He fears they would stop him or punish him.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am afraid of the government.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the remedy can actually be carried out.
steps.kashyaTarget: The advice to rebuild the בית המקדש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רומי might forbid it, so he cannot do it.

steps.title: Send a messenger and build in the meantime
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא suggests sending a messenger to רומי. The round trip will take three years, enough time to tear down and rebuild. הורדוס does this.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Send a messenger. Let him travel a year, stay a year, and come back a year. Meanwhile you can tear it down and rebuild it. He did so.
steps.whatsHappening: בבא בן בוטא gives a clever plan to get past the problem with רומי, and הורדוס follows it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking permission keeps הורדוס looking loyal, and the slow journey gives him time. By the time an answer comes back, the work is done.

phrases.english: He said to him: Send a messenger;

phrases.aramaic: וְלֵיזִיל שַׁתָּא, וְלִיעַכַּב שַׁתָּא, וְלֶהְדַּר שַׁתָּא;
phrases.english: let him travel a year, stay a year, and return a year;
in the meantime you can tear it down and build it.
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets ('it') are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: He did so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the fear in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A practical plan that uses the delay.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fear of רומי makes rebuilding impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ask permission, and finish the work before the answer comes back.

steps.title: רומי's angry reply to הורדוס
steps.stepSummary: רומי writes to הורדוס: don't tear it down, don't rebuild, and if you did both, you acted wickedly. They add that he is no king, only a former slave who made himself free.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent to him: If you have not torn it down, don't. If you tore it down, don't rebuild. If you tore it down and rebuilt it, you are among the wicked who act first and ask afterward. Though you have weapons, your records are here: you are neither a king nor a king's son, but Herod, a slave who made himself free.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רומי's reply, which comes too late to stop the building.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three-part letter shows the plan worked, since the answer arrived after the work was done. The insult about being a slave matches הורדוס calling himself the 'evil slave' earlier in the story.

keyTerms.meaning: a freed man (a slave who became free)

steps.whatToRemember: The guilt of killing the חכמים led הורדוס to rebuild the בית המקדש, following בבא בן בוטא's advice. רומי's late reply shows the plan succeeded.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ: אִם לֹא סָתַרְתָּה – אַל תִּסְתּוֹר;
phrases.english: They sent to him: If you have not torn it down, do not tear it down;
phrases.notes: 'They' are the Roman rulers.

phrases.english: and if you have torn it down, do not build it;
and if you have torn it down and built it,
wicked servants ask for advice after they have already acted.
If your weapons are upon you, your book is here:
phrases.notes: They mean: you may have an army, but we have your family records.

phrases.english: neither a king nor the son of a king,
Herod the slave has made himself a free man.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets ('slave') is added in the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ: אִם לֹא סָתַרְתָּה אַל תִּסְתּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows what happened after the plan in step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: הורדוס rebuilt the בית המקדש before רומי could stop him, and רומי replied by calling him a former slave and not a true king.

steps.title: What does the word רכא mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word רכא in רומי's letter means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'רכא' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about a hard word in the letter from רומי. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The letter said that הורדוס is neither a רכא nor the son of a רכא. To understand the insult, we first need to know what רכא means.

keyTerms.meaning: A word from the letter; the גמרא is about to explain it

phrases.english: What is 'reikha'?
phrases.notes: This word comes from the letter רומי sent, which said הורדוס is not a רכא and not the son of a רכא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a word from the letter quoted in step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word רכא.

steps.title: רכא means royalty, proven from a פסוק about דוד
steps.stepSummary: רכא means מלכות, as seen from a פסוק where 'רך' describes a king.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means royalty, as it is written: 'I am today רך and an anointed king.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: רכא means royalty, and brings a פסוק to show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the word רך stands right next to 'anointed king', so it is a word connected to kingship. So the letter meant: הורדוס is not a king and not the son of a king.

keyTerms.meaning: Soft or tender; here linked to being king

phrases.english: Royalty, as it is written:
"I am today tender and anointed king."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 3:39

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רכא means מלכות, as shown from the פסוק 'אנכי היום רך ומשוח מלך'.

steps.title: A second source: what they called out before יוסף
steps.stepSummary: Another proof that רכא means royalty: they called out 'אברך' before יוסף when he was made a ruler.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is learned from here: 'And they called out before him, אברך.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another פסוק to show the same meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When יוסף was made ruler under פרעה, people called out 'אברך' before him. The word holds the letters of רך, showing that this root connects to ruling. The meaning stays the same; only the source changes.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another option)
A title called out before יוסף

phrases.english: And if you wish, say from here:
"And they cried before him, Avrekh."
phrases.notes: בראשית 41:43, said about יוסף.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second proof for the same answer as step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The meaning 'royalty' can also be learned from 'ויקראו לפניו אברך'.

steps.title: No building was more beautiful than הורדוס's
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say that anyone who did not see הורדוס's building never saw a beautiful building.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Whoever has not seen הורדוס's building has never seen a beautiful building in his life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to praise the building הורדוס made, the בית המקדש he rebuilt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though הורדוס was wicked, the building he made was famous for being very beautiful. This opens a short description of how it was built.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: מִי שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה בִּנְיַן הוֹרְדוֹס,
phrases.english: They say: One who has not seen Herod's building,
has never seen a beautiful building in his life.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording; some versions don't have it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי מִי שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה בִּנְיַן הוֹרְדוֹס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the letter of רומי to describing the building הורדוס actually made.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הורדוס's building was the most beautiful building one could see.

steps.title: What did he build it with?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what materials הורדוס used.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what did he build it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the building was made from. This sets up the answer of רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After saying the building was so beautiful, the natural next question is what made it look that way.

phrases.english: With what did he build it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for details about the building praised in step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The building materials of הורדוס's building.

steps.title: Built from marble stones
steps.stepSummary: רבה says it was built from green and white marble; others add blue marble.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: With stones of green and white marble. Some say: With stones of blue, green and white marble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the building was made from marble, with two versions of which colors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions agree it was marble. The second version adds a third, blue kind of stone.

keyTerms.meaning: Green marble stones, as Rashi explains

phrases.english: Rabba said: With stones of green and white marble.
There are those who say:
With stones of blue, green, and white marble.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It was built of marble: white and green, or according to others blue, white and green.

steps.title: How the stones were laid
steps.stepSummary: The rows of stones stuck out a bit and went in a bit, so they would hold the plaster.
steps.simpleTranslation: He made an edge stick out and an edge go in, so that it would hold the plaster.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא describes how the stones were set in the wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some rows stuck out a little and some were set back a little. This uneven edge helped the plaster stay on.

phrases.english: He sent out an edge and drew in an edge,
so that it would receive the plaster.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds how the stones from step 21 were arranged.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stones were laid in alternating rows, out and in, to hold the plaster.

steps.title: The חכמים tell him not to cover it with gold
steps.stepSummary: הורדוס wanted to cover the stones with gold, but the חכמים said it looked better as it was, like waves of the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought to cover it with gold. The רבנן said to him: Leave it, because it is more beautiful this way, since it looks like the waves of the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the description of the building with the advice of the רבנן not to cover it with gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain marble, with rows going in and out, looked like sea waves. The רבנן felt gold would hide this beauty.
steps.whatToRemember: הורדוס's בית המקדש was made of marble laid in rows that looked like sea waves, and the רבנן told him to leave it without gold.

phrases.english: He thought to cover it with gold,
the Rabbis said to him: Leave it,
since it is more beautiful this way,
as it looks like the waves of the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the description of the building.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The building was left without gold because the marble looked like sea waves.

steps.title: How could בבא בן בוטא give advice to הורדוס, when דניאל was punished for advising נבוכדנצר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges בבא בן בוטא's advice to הורדוס from the case of דניאל, who was punished for advising נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did בבא בן בוטא do this? But רב יהודה said in the name of רב, and some say רבי יהושע בן לוי: Why was דניאל punished? Because he gave advice to נבוכדנצר, as it says: 'Therefore, O king, let my advice please you: redeem your sins with charity and your wrongs with kindness to the poor, so your peace may be lengthened.' And it says: 'All this came upon King נבוכדנצר,' and it says: 'At the end of twelve months.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the story and asks how בבא בן בוטא was allowed to give advice to the wicked הורדוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דניאל advised the wicked king נבוכדנצר to give charity, and the פסוקים show the decree against נבוכדנצר came only after twelve months, so the advice helped him. Since דניאל was punished for helping a wicked king, how could בבא בן בוטא help הורדוס?
steps.confusionAlert: דניאל's advice was good advice (give charity). The problem was not bad advice, but that he helped a wicked king keep his success.

phrases.aramaic: וּבָבָא בַּר בּוּטָא הֵיכִי עֲבַד הָכִי?
phrases.english: And how did Bava ben Buta do this?
phrases.notes: He means: how could he give advice to הורדוס, as in steps 11 to 14.

phrases.english: But doesn't Rav Yehuda say that Rav says,
and some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi:
For what reason was Daniel punished?
Because he gave advice to Nebuchadnezzar,
as it is stated: "Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you,
phrases.notes: דניאל 4:24

phrases.english: and redeem your sins with charity,
and your iniquities with graciousness to the poor,
that there may be a lengthening of your prosperity, etc."
And it is written: "All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar,"
phrases.notes: דניאל 4:25

phrases.english: And it is written: "And at the end of twelve months, etc."
phrases.notes: דניאל 4:26. The decree came only a year later, which shows דניאל's advice helped the king.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבָבָא בַּר בּוּטָא הֵיכִי עֲבַד הָכִי וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the building description to challenge בבא בן בוטא's advice in steps 11-14.
steps.kashyaTarget: בבא בן בוטא's advice to הורדוס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: דניאל was punished for advising a wicked king; so too בבא בן בוטא should not have advised the wicked הורדוס.

steps.title: A slave is obligated in מצוות
steps.stepSummary: First answer: הורדוס was a slave, and a slave is obligated in מצוות, unlike נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: A slave is different, because he is obligated in מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a first answer that separates הורדוס from נבוכדנצר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הורדוס was a slave, as the letter from רומי said, and a slave has a duty to keep מצוות. So guiding him toward תשובה was proper, unlike giving advice to נבוכדנצר, who had no such obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (first possible answer)

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
A slave is different, since he is obligated in מצוות.
phrases.notes: The slave here is הורדוס, who was earlier called a slave who freed himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the person: הורדוס is unlike נבוכדנצר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Advising any wicked ruler is forbidden, as with דניאל.
steps.terutzMaskana: A slave is obligated in מצוות, so advising him is different.

steps.title: The בית המקדש is different
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the בית המקדש could not be built without the government, so advising the king was allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: The בית המקדש is different, because without the government it would not be built.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer: the purpose of the advice was special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not focus on who הורדוס was, but on what the advice was for. Building the בית המקדש needed the power of the מלכות, so advising the king for that goal was allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: Two reasons allowed בבא בן בוטא to advise הורדוס: הורדוס as a slave was obligated in מצוות, or the בית המקדש could only be built with the government's help.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
The Temple is different,
as without the government it would not have been built.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different answer to the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the purpose: the advice was for building the בית המקדש.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Advising any wicked ruler is forbidden, as with דניאל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Advice needed to get the בית המקדש built is allowed, since it could not be built without the government.

steps.title: How do we know דניאל was punished?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that דניאל was punished for advising נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And דניאל, how do we know he was punished?
steps.whatsHappening: Step 24 assumed that דניאל was punished. Now the גמרא asks where we actually learn that from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole challenge against בבא בן בוטא depended on דניאל having been punished. So the גמרא wants a clear source that this really happened.

phrases.english: And Daniel, from where do we know that he was punished?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to check the assumption behind the challenge in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that דניאל was punished for his advice to נבוכדנצר.

steps.title: A suggested source: התך is דניאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the proof comes from the פסוק about התך, since רב says התך is דניאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is because it is written, "And אסתר called for התך," and רב said that התך is דניאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible proof. In מגילת אסתר, דניאל appears as a simple servant named התך, which would show he was demoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that going from a great minister to a lowly attendant was itself his punishment. The proof depends on how we understand the name התך.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion the גמרא may reject)
Hatach, a servant in מגילת אסתר whom רב identifies as דניאל

phrases.english: If you say it is because it is written:
"And Esther called for Hatach,"
phrases.notes: אסתר 4:5

phrases.english: and Rav said: Hatach is Daniel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first possible answer to the question of step 27.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in אסתר together with רב's statement that התך is דניאל.

steps.title: The proof only works by one explanation of the name
steps.stepSummary: If the name התך means he was cut down from his greatness, the proof works. If it means all government matters were decided by him, there is no proof of punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says he was called התך because they cut him down from his greatness. But according to the one who says it is because all the kingdom's matters were decided by his word, what can you say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggested proof. One opinion explains the name התך as praise, not as a demotion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word חתך can mean "cut down" or "decided." By the second meaning, the name shows that דניאל was powerful, not punished. So the proof falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well (according to one view)

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says:
"that they cut him down from his greatness,"
phrases.notes: The name התך sounds like חתך, "cut."

phrases.english: but according to the one who says:
"that all matters of the kingdom
were decided by his word,"
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the proof in step 28 does not work for everyone.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from the name התך.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By one explanation, the name shows power and not a demotion, so there is no sign of punishment.

steps.title: His punishment was the lions' den
steps.stepSummary: The real punishment was that דניאל was thrown into the lions' den.
steps.simpleTranslation: That they threw him into the den of lions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a source that works for everyone: דניאל was thrown to the lions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the name התך cannot prove a punishment for everyone, the גמרא points to a different event. Being thrown into the lions' den was his punishment for the advice he gave.
steps.whatToRemember: דניאל was punished, at least through the lions' den. That is why the גמרא needed special answers (steps 25-26) to explain why בבא בן בוטא was allowed to advise הורדוס.

phrases.english: That they threw him into the den of lions.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem of step 29 by giving a different proof.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the התך proof, there might be no evidence that דניאל was punished.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lions' den shows that he was punished.

steps.title: What does the word "everything" add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and asks what the word הכל comes to include.
steps.simpleTranslation: Everything follows the custom of the region. What does "everything" come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The side story is over, and the גמרא returns to the משנה about building the wall. It asks why the משנה added the word הכל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already listed the types of stone and brick. So the extra word הכל seems to be teaching something more.

phrases.english: Everything is according to the custom of the region.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: "Everything": to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story of דניאל and goes back to explaining the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra case the word הכל adds.

steps.title: It adds a place that uses palm and laurel branches
steps.stepSummary: הכל includes a place where people make partitions from palm and laurel branches.
steps.simpleTranslation: To include a place where people are used to building with palm branches and laurel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even a flimsy, branch-made partition is required if that is the local custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The listed materials were all stone or brick. הכל teaches that local custom decides even when the custom is a much weaker material.

phrases.english: To include a place
where they are accustomed to use palm branches and laurel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: הכל adds a place where partitions are made from palm and laurel branches.

steps.title: Isn't it obvious that a fallen wall belongs to both?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that a fallen wall's space and stones belong to both neighbors, and asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, if the wall fell, the space and the stones belong to both of them. That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and complains that it seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both neighbors built the wall together, so of course they share it. Why would the משנה need to teach this?

phrases.english: Therefore, if the wall fell,
the space and the stones belong to both of them.
It's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the משנה's ruling that a fallen wall belongs to both.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: They built it together, so sharing it is self-evident.

steps.title: Needed when the stones are on one side
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed when the wall fell into one neighbor's property, or one neighbor moved the stones to his side. Even then, the other does not have to bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where the wall fell into one of their properties, or where one of them cleared the stones into his own property. You might have said that the other one is a claimant who must bring proof. The משנה teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point: even if the stones are now sitting on one person's land, they still belong to both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, someone who wants to take something from another person's possession must bring proof (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה). The משנה teaches that here we already assume they were partners, so no proof is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for a special case)
Whoever wants to take something from another must bring proof

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that whoever holds the stones keeps them. Here, the shared building of the wall is enough to show joint ownership.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where it fell into the property of one of them,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי דְּפַנִּינְהוּ חַד לִרְשׁוּתָא דִידֵיהּ;
phrases.english: or alternatively, where one of them cleared them into his own property;
you might have said:
let the other one be
"one who takes from his fellow bears the burden of proof,"
so it teaches us.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דִּנְפַל לִרְשׁוּתָא דְּחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the rule to a special case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The neighbor without the stones must prove he owns part of them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are assumed to be partners, and no proof is needed.

steps.title: The garden ruling seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the garden ruling and begins to show a contradiction inside it. The first half implies that with no custom, there is no obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And similarly in a garden, in a place where people are used to fencing, they obligate him. This itself is difficult. You said: in a garden where people are used to fencing, they obligate him. That implies that ordinarily, they do not obligate him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a garden and starts pointing out a problem. This step sets up the first side of a contradiction, and the other side comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the משנה mentions a place with a custom to fence, it seems that a place with no custom has no obligation. The גמרא will next show that the משנה's later wording seems to say the opposite.

keyTerms.meaning: To fence or build a partition
This itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)

phrases.english: And similarly in a garden,
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: in a place where they are accustomed to fence,
they obligate him.
This itself is difficult:
you said: and similarly in a garden,
in a place where they are accustomed to fence, they obligate him;
which implies that ordinarily, they do not obligate him;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the garden line of the משנה and begins a new challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the משנה's garden ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause implies there is no obligation without a custom. The contrasting inference from the later clause comes in step 36.

steps.title: The second half of the garden ruling clashes with the first half
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא about a field implies that in an ordinary field with no custom, a partition is required. The רישא implied that an ordinary garden needs no partition. That makes no sense, because a garden needs privacy more than a field does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the second half: 'But a field, where the custom is not to fence, they do not obligate him.' That implies that in an ordinary field, they do obligate him. But you already implied that an ordinary garden needs no partition. Do we even need to say that an ordinary field needs none?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the contradiction it started in step 35. It shows that the second half of the משנה implies the opposite of the first half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the רישא we learned that an ordinary גינה, with no custom, needs no partition. From the סיפא we learn that an ordinary בקעה does need one. Since a garden needs protection from prying eyes more than a field, it is backwards to say the field is stricter.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter part of the משנה
Ordinarily, a plain case with no special custom
Is it even necessary to say?

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בִּקְעָה, מְקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִגְדּוֹר –
phrases.english: But a field, in a place where they are accustomed not to fence –
they do not obligate him;
this implies that ordinarily – they do obligate him.
phrases.notes: 'Ordinarily' means a place with no custom either way.

phrases.english: Now, for an ordinary garden – you said no,
is it necessary to say so for an ordinary field?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contradiction begun in step 35
steps.kashyaTarget: The garden-and-field clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא implies that an ordinary garden needs no partition, and the סיפא implies that an ordinary field does. That ranks a field above a garden, which is backwards.

steps.title: אביי reads the ordinary garden as obligated
steps.stepSummary: אביי reads the משנה as saying that both an ordinary garden and a field in a fencing-custom place require a partition.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said that this is what the משנה means: likewise an ordinary garden, and a field in a place where the custom is to fence, they obligate him.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by rereading the משנה. In his reading, an ordinary garden does require a partition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contradiction came from reading the garden rule as applying only where there is a custom. אביי makes the garden rule apply even with no custom. He then joins the custom-to-fence field to the same rule, so nothing contradicts anymore.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what the text means

phrases.english: Abaye said, this is what it is saying:
And likewise an ordinary garden,
and in a place where they are accustomed to fence in a field –
they obligate him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 36
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The garden rule applies only where there is a fencing custom
steps.terutzMaskana: An ordinary garden is obligated, and so is a field in a fencing-custom place

steps.title: רבא objects to the word 'אבל'
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks why the משנה says 'אבל' (but) about a field if fields were already covered in the earlier clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If so, what is the point of the word 'but'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges אביי's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's reading, the field case already appears in the first clause. 'אבל' signals a new, contrasting topic. That only fits if fields were not mentioned before.

keyTerms.meaning: But, a word that marks a contrast

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If so, what is the point of 'but'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's answer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'אבל' introduces a contrast with something new. Under אביי's reading, the field case was already covered.

steps.title: רבא: an ordinary garden counts as a fencing place, an ordinary field does not
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads the משנה as setting default rules. An ordinary garden is treated like a fencing-custom place and is obligated. An ordinary field is treated like a no-fencing place and is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said that this is what the משנה teaches: an ordinary garden is like a place where they fence, so they obligate him. But an ordinary field is like a place where they do not fence, so they do not obligate him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own reading of the משנה. In his reading, 'אבל' fits nicely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each kind of land gets a default for when there is no custom. The garden defaults to 'fence' and the field defaults to 'no fence'. Now 'אבל' introduces a real contrast between the two, and the garden is stricter, which makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what the משנה teaches
Is treated like, is comparable to

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא: with no custom, a garden needs a partition but a field does not.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said, this is what it teaches:
And likewise an ordinary garden –
is treated like a place where they are accustomed to fence,
and they obligate him.
But an ordinary field –
is treated like a place where they are not accustomed to fence,
and they do not obligate him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's reading, which רבא rejected in step 38
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the משנה as setting default rules
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ordinary cases are judged only by local custom
steps.terutzMaskana: An ordinary garden defaults to obligated, and an ordinary field defaults to not obligated

steps.title: What is the חזית mentioned in the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line about building on one's own land and making a חזית, and asks what a חזית is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'Rather, if he wants, he moves into his own land, builds, and makes a חזית.' What is a חזית?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next line of the משנה. It asks what the unclear word חזית means, which sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who builds a wall alone on his own land needs a sign showing the wall is entirely his. The גמרא wants to know what this sign physically looks like.

keyTerms.meaning: Moves inward, pulls back onto his own land
A visible border mark on the wall

phrases.english: Rather, if he wants,
he moves into his own land and builds,
and makes a border mark.
What is a 'border mark'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the next line of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word חזית

steps.title: רב הונא: bend the wall's edge outward
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא explains that the חזית means bending the corner of the wall toward the outside, the neighbor's side.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: He bends the edge of the wall toward the outside.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers what a חזית is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The builder bends the edge of the wall so it sticks out toward the neighbor's side. This shape shows that the whole wall belongs to the builder.

keyTerms.meaning: The edge or corner of the wall

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
He bends the edge toward the outside.
phrases.notes: 'Outside' here means the side facing the neighbor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 40
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The edge of the wall is bent outward

steps.title: Why not bend it inward?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the mark isn't made on the inside, the builder's own side.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make it on the inside!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's choice of the outer side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bending the edge toward his own side would seem simpler. It would also keep the wall from sticking out toward the neighbor.

phrases.english: Let him make it on the inside!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רב הונא's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's choice of the outer side
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An inner mark seems to work just as well.

steps.title: An inner mark lets the neighbor add his own mark
steps.stepSummary: If the mark were inside, the neighbor could make a matching mark on his side and claim the wall is shared.
steps.simpleTranslation: His neighbor could also make a mark on the outside and say: It is mine and his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the mark cannot go on the inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With marks on both sides, the wall would look like it was built together. If the mark is on the outside, the neighbor's only trick would be to cut it off. The גמרא tests that idea in the next two steps.

phrases.english: His neighbor would also make one on the outside,
and say: It is mine and his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 42
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a risk of cheating
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An inner mark would be enough
steps.terutzMaskana: An inner mark can be copied by the neighbor on his side

steps.title: The neighbor could cut off an outer mark
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back that even an outer mark could be cut off by the neighbor, who would then claim the wall is shared.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, now too his neighbor could cut it off and say: It is mine and his!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא argues that the outer mark has the same weakness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we worry the neighbor will cheat, he could cheat here too by cutting away the bent edge. So the outer mark seems no safer.

phrases.english: If so, now too –
his neighbor could cut it off,
and say: It is mine and his!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the cheating worry back against the outer mark
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A neighbor willing to cheat can cut off the outer mark just as easily.

steps.title: A cut can be noticed
steps.stepSummary: Cutting off the mark leaves visible traces, so the trick would be caught.
steps.simpleTranslation: A cut is noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that cutting cannot be hidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding a new mark on one's own side leaves nothing suspicious. But shaving off part of a wall leaves clear signs of damage. So the outer mark is safe.
steps.whatToRemember: First version: the חזית is bent outward, because a cut-off mark would be noticed.

phrases.english: A cut is noticeable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 44
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical difference between the two cheating methods
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting is as easy to hide as adding
steps.terutzMaskana: Cutting leaves visible signs, so an outer mark is safe

steps.title: Second version: רב הונא says bend the edge inward
steps.stepSummary: Some report that רב הונא said the חזית is bending the edge toward the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רב הונא said: He bends the edge toward the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of what רב הונא said, which gives the opposite answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the mark is on the builder's own side instead of the neighbor's side. The same back-and-forth will now run in reverse.

phrases.english: There are those who say, Rav Huna said:
Bending the edge toward the inside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different version of רב הונא's answer to step 40
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The edge of the wall is bent inward

steps.title: Why not bend it outward?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the mark isn't made on the outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make it on the outside!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the inner mark in this second version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An outer mark seems like a clear sign of who owns the wall. So why choose the inside?

phrases.english: Let him make it on the outside!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the second version
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An outer mark seems to work.

steps.title: An outer mark could be cut off
steps.stepSummary: An outer mark is within the neighbor's reach, so he could cut it off and claim the wall is shared.
steps.simpleTranslation: His neighbor could cut it off and say: It is mine and his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why this version avoids an outer mark.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the worry is that the neighbor will remove a mark on his side. A mark on the builder's side is out of his reach.

phrases.english: His neighbor could cut it off,
and say: It is mine and his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 47
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a risk of cheating
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An outer mark would be enough
steps.terutzMaskana: An outer mark can be cut off by the neighbor

steps.title: The neighbor could add a matching mark
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back that with an inner mark, the neighbor could add a matching mark on his own side.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, now too his neighbor could add one and say: It is mine and his!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא argues that the inner mark has its own weakness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we worry about cheating, the neighbor could make a matching mark on his side. Then the wall would look like it was built together.

phrases.english: If so, now too
his neighbor could add one,
and say: It is mine and his!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the cheating worry back against the inner mark
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A cheating neighbor could add a matching mark on his side.

steps.title: An addition can be noticed
steps.stepSummary: A newly added piece would look different from the original wall, so the trick would be caught.
steps.simpleTranslation: An addition is noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that adding on cannot be hidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of the first version. Here, adding is easy to spot. In the first version, cutting was easy to spot.

keyTerms.meaning: An addition attached to the wall

steps.confusionAlert: The two versions disagree about which trick can be noticed. The first says a cut is noticeable, and the second says an addition is noticeable. Don't mix them up.

phrases.english: An addition is noticeable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 49
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical difference between the two cheating methods
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Adding is as easy to hide as cutting
steps.terutzMaskana: An added piece is visible, so an inner mark is safe

steps.title: The משנה says 'on the outside'
steps.stepSummary: The second version clashes with the משנה, which says the mark is made 'מבחוץ' (on the outside).
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches 'on the outside'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second version using the exact words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: However sensible the reasoning is, the משנה clearly places the חזית on the outside. An inner mark contradicts the text.

keyTerms.meaning: On the outside, the word used in the משנה

phrases.english: But it teaches 'on the outside'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second version as a whole
steps.kashyaTarget: The second version of רב הונא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה explicitly places the mark on the outside, not the inside.

steps.title: The difficulty remains
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves the challenge unanswered. The second version stands refuted by the wording of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer for the second version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קשיא' means the question stands and no answer is given. Only the second version of רב הונא, with the edge bent inward, is left with this difficulty. The first version, with the edge bent outward, fits the word מבחוץ.

keyTerms.meaning: A difficulty that is left unanswered

steps.whatToRemember: The inner-mark version of רב הונא is left with an unanswered difficulty because the משנה says מבחוץ. The outer-mark version has no such problem, and רבי יוחנן's explanation comes next.

phrases.english: It is a difficulty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge in step 51 without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The second version contradicts the משנה, and the difficulty is left standing.

steps.title: Introducing רבי יוחנן's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new statement in the name of רבי יוחנן about the marking on the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It introduces רבי יוחנן, who is about to give his own explanation, and his actual words come right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second version was just knocked down because it clashed with the word מבחוץ in the משנה. So the גמרא turns to a new אמורא who offers a different way to understand the marking. Nothing has been ruled yet; this line only says who is speaking.

keyTerms.meaning: The marking on the wall that shows who owns it, which is the subject under discussion

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a full statement on its own. Don't look for a ruling here. רבי יוחנן's actual words come right after it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the second version was refuted in Step 52, the גמרא turns to a different אמורא's explanation of the marking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line only introduces רבי יוחנן, whose explanation of the marking follows.
